Initial winds northwesterly at low altitude (300-500m); stable nocturnal atmosphere; upper atmosphere SE winds 8-10 m/s at 1500m; high pressure over western Siberia driving northward transport

Forsmark Nuclear Power Plant workers found with radioactive particles on clothing ~1100 km from Chernobyl; triggered international awareness; Swedish authorities alerted Soviet Union; USSR denied accident initially
Poland: radioactivity 550,000 times higher than baseline on April 28; Poland was the only country to distribute KI to population (~18 million people) in the first days
Wind shifted from southeast to westerly direction April 28-29; plume path changed direction; second radioactive cloud path through Slovakia Czech Republic Austria
Second radioactive cloud path reaches Slovakia, Czech Republic, Austria; Hungary sharp rise in radioactivity recorded
Plume reaches southern Germany; entire region affected; high pressure formed over North Europe changed wind to southerly; Bavaria received significant deposition
Northerly winds became effective April 30; changed overall transport pattern; subsequent plume pulses tracked differently
Plume traveled to Ireland May 1-2; minimal precipitation (0.0-0.5 mm); low deposition; no milk ban triggered initially
source: Met Eireann; EPA Ireland; Kilkenny Weather archives

notes: Plume arrived with significant rainfall May 3 (5.1 mm); maximum deposition event; wet deposition 50-100x more efficient than dry; triggered milk monitoring
Peak milk contamination in Ireland: 441 Bq/L I-131 on May 5; triggered concern but no national milk ban; Irish action level was 2000 Bq/L
Lamb samples: 1155 Bq/kg; elevated but monitoring continued
Peak rainfall period May 4-6 (7.9-8.9 mm daily); maximum fallout deposited; 99% of total deposition during this period in some western European locations
Magdeburg Germany: thunderstorm May 5 brought down highly concentrated plume; grass 75000 Bq/kg I-131; storm water 44000 Bq/L; garden soil 40000 Bq/kg; extreme localized deposition
Weakened plume passed south of Ireland May 7; lower deposition (3.1 mm rain); monitoring continued but lower levels
Graphite fire extinguished approximately May 9 1986 (some sources say May 5-6); end of major high-altitude release; residual volatilization continued but much reduced

Only ~1% deposition in dry form during April 27 to May 8; ~99% deposited during precipitation events; rainfall governed by orders of magnitude where contamination fell; explains patchy deposition pattern

Specific locations received 99% of total deposition in single 12-hour rain event May 8; activity concentration in rainwater decreased by factor ~50 from start to end of rain as plume washed out; geographic determinism of rainfall

First plume path (Apr 26-30): NW winds carried activity to Scandinavia, Finland, Baltic states, Netherlands, Belgium, UK. Sweden first to detect externally (April 28 Forsmark). Finland, Denmark, Norway detected April 28-29.

Second plume path (Apr 29 - May 5): wind shift carried plume southwestward; Poland, Czech Republic, Austria, southern Germany, Switzerland, northern Italy affected; alpine rainfall caused high deposition in some mountain areas

Third plume path (May 1-10): changed wind pattern carried plume westward to France, UK, Ireland; some activity reached North America (trace levels) and Japan (below significance); global dispersion of noble gases (Xe-133 100% released)

6500 PBq Xe-133 (noble gas, 100% core release); dispersed globally in ~30 days; detected at monitoring stations worldwide including Japan and USA; no direct dose but used as atmospheric tracer for plume tracking

Cs-134/Cs-137 activity ratio = 0.57 ± 0.07 (decay-corrected to May 6 1986); characteristic of Unit 4 fuel burnup of ~10 GWd/tU; used to distinguish Chernobyl contamination from weapons testing fallout (testing has different ratio); also used to detect 1986 vs 2017 Ru-106 episode
